name: Volume guarantee
use: A commitment to buy, or pay for, a minimum volume if demand falls short, in exchange for a lower price or new capacity.
holds: Demand proves real, so the guarantee is not drawn on, and volume persists at the new price.
example: Contraceptive implants in 2013 and TLD in 2017.
watch: Payouts count as costs. A guarantee that keeps being called suggests a structural gap.
strengths: Low expected cost when demand is real
Suppliers still earn from sales to buyers
Expires unused if demand turns out to be real
limitations: Needs a reliable demand forecast
Set at the wrong volume, it can mislead suppliers about demand

name: Advance market commitment
levers: Risk transfer, scale, with a capped long-term price
use: A promise to pay a set price, often with a premium for early units, for products that meet specified criteria, paid only when they are delivered.
holds: The long-term price commitment is honored after the premium is spent, and buyers keep buying.
example: The 2009 pneumococcal vaccine commitment, and Frontier for carbon removal.
watch: Where the product already exists, the counterfactual is murky and a guarantee or ceiling price may bring supply forward as quickly for less.
strengths: Brings forward investment in capacity or development
Gives manufacturers a known price
Pays only on delivery
limitations: Requires a large commitment
Complex to design and administer
Counterfactual is hard to establish when the product already exists

name: Ceiling price agreement
use: A negotiated maximum price that buyers can tender beneath, often paired with a guarantee.
holds: Enough suppliers stay viable at or below the ceiling to keep competing.
example: TLD at about $75 per patient per year in 2017.
watch: Suppliers exit if the ceiling is too low and charge it if it is too high.
strengths: No capital required on its own
Allows competitive tenders beneath the ceiling
Gives buyers price certainty for planning
limitations: Hard to set at the right level
Usually needs volume assurance to be credible

name: Voluntary licensing
use: An originator licenses generic manufacturers to produce for specified markets, often through a patent pool.
holds: Licensed suppliers stay viable at the lower price. Thin margins often lead to exits and consolidation, which weakens competition.
example: The Medicines Patent Pool provided the licensing channel for generic TLD.
watch: Territorial limits can exclude middle-income markets where the gap is real.
strengths: Brings in generic competition without donor capital
Can cover many countries at once
limitations: Territorial limits can exclude middle-income markets
Depends on the originator agreeing to license

name: Technical assistance and process engineering
use: Expert work with suppliers on production processes, sourcing and cost structure, usually under confidentiality.
holds: Suppliers keep what they learn, which makes this the most durable lever.
example: The 2003 generic antiretroviral agreements, which cut a common triple-therapy pill from about $300 to under $140 per patient per year.
watch: Requires industrial engineering capability, access to supplier cost data and supplier trust, so it depends heavily on who does it.
strengths: Improvements stay with the supplier
Lowers the supplier's underlying production costs
A small grant can lower prices across a large market
limitations: Takes a lot of expert time
Works only if suppliers can take up the changes
Hard to measure without cost data

name: Market intelligence
use: Publishing prices, suppliers, forecasts and costs so buyers can bargain and suppliers can plan.
holds: Someone keeps producing it. Information is a public good, so it needs a small continuing payer of its own.
example: Public price and supplier reports for HIV and other commodities.
watch: Its value depends on buyers using it, so measure it by the decisions it changes.
strengths: Benefits every buyer and supplier who uses it
Relatively low cost
Helps buyers bargain and suppliers plan
limitations: Needs continuing funding
Suppliers and buyers may not share their data

name: Pooled procurement
use: Aggregating demand across buyers into fewer, larger, more predictable orders.
holds: The pool persists. If buyers leave, volume and bargaining power go with them.
example: Common in vaccine and HIV commodity markets.
watch: Can concentrate supply on few manufacturers and weaken resilience.
strengths: Larger orders can lower prices substantially
Quality assurance
Fewer, larger tenders cost less to run
limitations: Requires coordination among buyers
May reduce supplier diversity

name: Payment guarantee
use: Covers suppliers if a buyer pays late or not at all, so they price without a credit-risk premium.
holds: Buyers prove creditworthy, so the premium does not return when the guarantee ends.
watch: Can hide a buyer's inability to pay, which only government or donor financing can address.
strengths: Lets suppliers serve higher-risk markets
Reduces the premium suppliers add for the risk of late payment
Makes suppliers more willing to enter
limitations: Requires reliable verification of delivery
Can hide whether a buyer is able to pay

name: Working capital and concessional debt
use: Below-market loans to suppliers or distributors, ideally tied to pricing or supply commitments.
holds: Cheaper capital stays available after the concession ends, which is often not the case.
watch: The saving lowers price only if it is passed into the contracted price.
strengths: Covers gaps between paying costs and receiving revenue
Can be tied to access commitments
Borrowers still have to repay
limitations: Borrowers must be able to repay
Lowers price only if the saving is passed through
May replace loans commercial lenders would have made

name: First-loss and loss-sharing guarantees for investors
use: A public or philanthropic party absorbs some losses so private lenders or investors will participate.
holds: Performance proves the risk lower than feared, so investors stay without the cover.
watch: First-loss (junior) and pari passu (proportional) cover transfer very different amounts of risk, so specify which.
strengths: A small amount of cover can bring in much larger private investment
Draws in commercial investors
Shows investors that the market can work
limitations: If badly designed, covered investors may take less care
May shift losses without reducing the risk behind them
Complex to structure

name: Price buy-down or subsidy
levers: None directly: a time-limited financial transfer
use: A third party pays part of the price for a fixed period, so buyers can afford more volume while costs fall.
holds: The volume it pays for lowers the underlying price, through scale, learning or new entrants, before the subsidy ends as planned.
example: Early solar feed-in tariffs, which paid above-market prices for a set period while costs fell.
watch: If the price rises again when the subsidy ends, it was in effect a permanent subsidy. Set the end date and the price target at the start.
strengths: Lowers the price at once
Simple to implement
Directly helps buyers who cannot afford the full price
limitations: Costly if the levers it relies on do not work
Hides the unsubsidized price while it runs
Ending it on schedule takes discipline

name: Outcome payments and impact bonds
use: A payer funds only verified results. In an impact bond, investors provide upfront capital and are repaid on results.
holds: The outcome payer keeps paying. The bond structure does not create a payer by itself.
example: In the Educate Girls development impact bond, the investor provided $270,000 and was repaid with a 15 percent return after targets were exceeded.
watch: Verifying results can cost more than the added accountability is worth.
strengths: Moves the risk of failure away from the payer
Focuses spending on results
Leaves providers free to choose their methods
limitations: High transaction and verification costs
Providers may game the measures
Not every outcome worth paying for is measurable

name: Subscription or delinked payment
use: A fixed payment for access, independent of volume sold.
holds: The payer keeps paying. By design, the market will not sustain itself.
example: Used for novel antibiotics, where stewardship should keep volumes low.
watch: Setting the payment requires an estimate of social value instead of a market price.
strengths: Gives developers predictable revenue
Removes the incentive to sell more than is needed
Simplifies planning
limitations: Requires an estimate of social value
Payer must commit for the long term

name: Corrective tax or compliance carbon price
levers: None directly: it raises the floor under the harmful activity
use: A price on a harmful activity, through a tax or a cap with tradable permits.
holds: The policy survives politically.
example: British Columbia priced carbon from 2008 until setting its consumer tax to zero in 2025.
watch: Include the chance of political reversal in the cost-effectiveness estimate.
strengths: Can cover the whole economy
Raises revenue
Corrects the externality at its source
limitations: Faces political resistance and can be reversed
Can put taxed firms at a disadvantage against untaxed competitors
Falls hardest on poorer households unless revenue is returned

name: Tax credits
use: Reduces tax owed per unit invested or produced.
holds: Costs fall below what buyers will pay. Otherwise the effect lasts only as long as the credit.
example: US wind and solar credits, curtailed by 2025 legislation for projects starting construction after July 4, 2026 and entering service after 2027.
watch: Only those with tax liability benefit, and a later law can end the credit.
strengths: Leaves investment decisions to firms
Can be applied at large scale
limitations: Benefits only those with tax liability
Costs the government revenue
A later law can end it

name: Innovation prize
levers: Innovation incentive, prior to the six levers
use: A reward paid to whoever first meets a defined technical goal.
holds: The prize gets a product made. Its price after that depends on the six levers.
watch: Pair with a downstream lever so the winning product reaches a sustainable access price.
strengths: A modest prize can draw much larger research spending
Pays only for meeting the goal
Draws entrants from outside the usual developers
limitations: Winner-take-all deters some entrants
The prize must match the difficulty of the goal
Does not set the access price

name: Parametric insurance
levers: Risk transfer, for governments rather than suppliers
use: Pays out automatically when an index, such as rainfall, crosses a threshold.
holds: Premiums keep being paid, often with donor subsidy.
example: African Risk Capacity had paid more than $170 million in claims by its tenth year.
watch: Basis risk: the index can miss real losses, or pay when there were none.
strengths: Pays out quickly
Cheap to administer
Payouts depend on a measured index
limitations: Basis risk: the index can miss real losses
A good index is hard to design

name: Offtake agreement
use: A buyer commits to purchase a project's output over many years at agreed prices, giving developers the revenue certainty that lenders require.
holds: Lenders and buyers come to treat the technology as bankable, so later projects can be financed without a committed buyer.
example: Long-term power purchase agreements financed early utility-scale solar and wind; Frontier's offtake contracts play the same role for carbon removal.
watch: It is the energy and climate counterpart of the volume guarantee. If the buyer is the only reason the project exists, the gap is probably structural.
strengths: Lets developers borrow against the contract
Can work at or near market prices
Familiar to commercial lenders
limitations: Needs a creditworthy buyer
Locks the buyer into long-term prices
An above-market price turns part of it into a transfer

name: Tiered pricing
money: No donor capital on its own
levers: None directly: a cross-subsidy from higher-income markets
use: A supplier charges lower prices in lower-income markets and recovers its fixed costs in higher-income ones.
holds: The supplier keeps an incentive to offer the low tier, which depends on keeping markets separate so the low price does not spread.
example: Widely used for vaccines sold to public buyers in low-income countries.
watch: A tiered price set by an originator is not a competitive price. Do not credit it for reductions that came from generic competition.
strengths: Requires no donor capital
Recovers fixed costs where buyers can pay
Can be agreed quickly
limitations: Depends on the supplier's goodwill and on separated markets
Middle-income countries can fall between tiers
Usually above the price competition would reach

name: Priority review vouchers and regulatory incentives
money: No donor capital: the value is created by a regulator
levers: Innovation incentive, prior to the six levers
use: A regulator grants something valuable, such as a voucher for faster review of another product, extended exclusivity or waived fees, to developers of products for neglected needs.
holds: Like other innovation incentives, it gets a product made. Its price and reach after that depend on the six levers.
example: The US Food and Drug Administration's priority review voucher for tropical diseases.
watch: A voucher rewards approval only. Pair it with access commitments or a downstream lever, or the product may launch at a price its target market cannot pay.
strengths: Costs donors nothing directly
Pays only for completion
Can attract large developers
limitations: The reward is unrelated to the product's social value
Approval does not guarantee access or affordability
The reward's value is uncertain

name: Voluntary carbon credits
use: Buyers pay for certified emission reductions or removals they are not required to make, usually to meet their own climate commitments.
holds: Buyers keep buying. Because their motives are mission and reputation, they are the least durable kind of payer.
example: Traded value peaked at around $2 billion in 2021 and fell to $535 million in 2024.
watch: Credits do not change what emitters pay, so they do not correct the externality. Check additionality and permanence, the market's main integrity problems.
strengths: Channels private money to activities no one else pays for
Can fund removal and conservation
Works across many sectors and countries
limitations: Buyers can stop buying at any time
Doubts about additionality and permanence
Does not change what emitters pay
